title: States take Meta to trial in California in the biggest fight yet over social media harms to children
description: Of the thousands of lawsuits Meta faces over child safety on its platforms, none may be more consequential than one going to trial this week in California.  States are seeking extensive financial dama...
fullText:
Of the thousands of lawsuits Meta faces over child safety on its platforms, none may be more consequential than one going to trial this week in California.

States are seeking extensive financial damages that could, in theory, total as much as $1.4 trillion, plus changes to how the company operates Facebook and Instagram.

The lawsuit accuses the social media giant of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly and deliberately designing features that get children addicted to its platforms. It also claims that Meta routinely collects data on children under 13 without their parents' consent, in violation of federal law.

"Meta has harnessed powerful and unprecedented technologies to entice, engage, and ultimately ensnare youth and teens. Its motive is profit, and in seeking to maximize its financial gains," the lawsuit says.

Dozens of states filed the lawsuit three years ago. The trial set to begin Tuesday in federal court in Oakland, California, features four of the states as plaintiffs — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. The other 25 states are expected to have trials later.

Meta said it disputes the allegations, and the trial evidence will show its commitment to supporting young people. "We've listened to parents, worked with experts and law enforcement, and conducted in-depth research to understand the issues that matter most," the company said in a statement.

For Meta, which already lost two pivotal cases over harms to children and teens this year, the stakes are high. The company reported a rare profit decline last month, in part due to $2.4 billion in legal expenses.

The $1.4 trillion figure, which Meta disclosed in a legal filing, is almost as high as the Menlo Park, California, company's entire market capitalization — that is, the value of all its outstanding shares on the stock market. Paying it would inevitably put Meta Platforms in bankruptcy and perhaps put the company under state ownership.

"The state attorneys general are going for the gusto," said Eric Goldman, a professor and co-director of the High Tech Law Institute at Santa Clara University School of Law. "They are trying to set the definitive precedent in this case and they have asked for extraordinary damages and they are going to seek extraordinary structural remedies if they succeed."

Meta calls the possible penalty "untethered to any claimed violation" by the states.

"A sanction of that size has no analog in the history of consumer protection enforcement," Meta said in a July 6 filing with the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.

If Meta loses the trial, the court would have wide discretion over the size of any financial penalty, and legal experts say anything close to $1.4 trillion would be unlikely.

"It's not plausible in the sense that Meta doesn't have that much money and could not get it," said James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Law School and Cornell Tech. "An award that large would put Meta into bankruptcy, wipe out its owners, and effectively result in the states owning Meta."

As a practical matter, Grimmelmann added, "that seems extremely unlikely to happen."

In other cases that have involved high potential damages for multiple individual offenses, he said courts have stopped short of imposing the maximum penalties. One example is the Anthropic artificial intelligence training case, where plaintiffs were claiming damages of $150,000 per book that Anthropic copied, but the penalty ended up being $3,000 per book, totaling about $1.5 billion.

The federal trial this week is more complex than one earlier this year, in Los Angeles, where a state court awarded $6 million in damages from Meta and Google's YouTube to a single plaintiff, a young woman who testified she became addicted to social media as a child.

That case was a bellwether, or test case, picked from thousands of similar civil tort lawsuits to give both plaintiffs and the defendants an idea of how their arguments fare in court. The jury determined that Meta and YouTube were negligent in the design or operation of their respective platforms, and that the negligence was a substantial factor in causing harm to the plaintiff. They also determined each company knew their platforms could be dangerous when used by a minor and that they failed to adequately warn of that danger.

The Oakland case, meanwhile, has state attorneys general as the plaintiffs and centers on state and federal statutes they allege Meta violated, which lay out potential penalty amounts for each violation.

"And there's a lot of them because it's four different states and at least three different kinds of statutes. There's a child privacy statute, there's a false advertising statute and there's unfair competition statutes," said Rebecca Allensworth, a professor at Vanderbilt University Law School.

An outcome that leads to changes in how Facebook and Instagram operate could be as consequential as any financial penalty.

Meta has introduced a slew of new features in recent years designed to protect minors. In 2024 it launched teen accounts on Instagram, which are private by default and come with messaging and content restrictions, and parental controls. The company also uses artificial intelligence to determine if kids under 13 are using Instagram or if teenagers are lying about their age to access adult accounts.

Safety advocates have called on the company to do more. A New Mexico judge earlier this month ordered new safety measures on the platforms including time limits for minors, AI chatbot restrictions, and mandatory warnings on the platforms, but his order applied only to users in the state.

"These AGs have a real chance at fixing the product," Laura Marquez-Garrett of the Social Media Victims Law Center said Friday in a virtual discussion with advocates hosted by the Tech Oversight Project. "For these companies, this is a real point of reckoning. As these cases go forward, this is a leap forward, folks, not a step."

During jury selection last week, prospective jurors were asked whether and how much they believe Meta has contributed to the youth mental health crisis. While many agreed that it did, they also put responsibility on parents, and said things like climate change and the state of the world are also causing children's and teenagers' mental health issues.

AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this report.

title: Berkeley math professor sounds alarm on liberal 'test-blind' policies, warns many students badly behind
description: A Berkeley professor attacked the University of California system's "test-blind" policies as calamitous, noting students were arriving on campus unable to do basic math.
fullText:
A Berkeley mathematics professor is sounding the alarm that many students are woefully unprepared when they arrive at college because the University of California system's progressive "test-blind" policies have proven disastrous.

"Three days a week, I stand in front of lecture halls with 500 to 1,400 students. By the second week of the semester, I already know who is in trouble," professor Zvezdelina Stankova wrote in a San Francisco Standard op-ed published Saturday.

"Some students are five to eight years behind in mathematics. Office hours that should be spent discussing integrals instead become lessons on fractions and basic algebra you would expect students to learn in middle school," he said.

Stankova and thousands of faculty members across the 10 UC campuses have signed open letters urging the university system to reinstate the SAT and ACT in admissions. Former UC president Janet Napolitano, who also served in the Obama administration, led the way in 2020 to phase out the standardized testing, in part out of "equity" concerns.

"Since then, admissions officers have been forbidden from considering the one standardized measure that provided a common academic benchmark across California's thousands of high schools," Stankova wrote.

Campus Antisemitism Extends Beyond Student Protests And Into Classrooms, Adl Warns

"After UC adopted test-blind admissions, the picture changed dramatically," she wrote.

Stankova laid out brutal data showing a sharp decline in student math readiness after UC stopped considering standardized tests. From 2018 to 2020, 71% of roughly 2,200 tested Calculus I students were deemed ready or nearly ready, while just 0.14% tested below basic algebra.

Among roughly 2,800 students tested from 2021 to 2023 using a different diagnostic, only 51% were ready or nearly ready. That fell to 44% in 2023, and a whopping 17% answered none of eight tested topics correctly.

"Those of us teaching such courses don't experience the consequences as abstractions. We watch students struggle through material they were expected to master years earlier. We pause lectures to reteach linear equations instead of expanding students' understanding of differential equations," Stankova wrote.

In an open letter from UC STEM faculty written in June, instructors specifically rejected the notion that "equity" was affected by the math requirement.

Ex-cambridge Professor Found Dead After Plagiarism Scandal Led To Abrupt Resignation

"The SAT/ACT mathematics requirement is not an obstacle to equity; rather, it is a prerequisite for it," they wrote. "Failing to measure preparation gaps does not remove barriers; it moves them into the classroom, where they become harder to overcome. An admissions process that ignores foundational readiness does a disservice to the most vulnerable students. True access requires an honest assessment of the support students need and where, within California's public higher education system, they can best receive it."

The UC announced that month it was launching a review of its standardized testing policy.

"The Board of Regents and University leadership take very seriously the critical issue of college preparedness, and the UC Academic Senate has proposed a comprehensive, data-driven review to support its recommendations to strengthen student readiness and success at UC," University of California President James B. Milliken said at the time. "There are few things more important on our agenda."

The op-ed comes as more elite universities are moving away from the test-optional policies that were in vogue during what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., might call the "Woke 1" era around 2020.

Conservatives Shred Aoc As She Attempts To Brush Off Radical 'Woke 1' Wave Amid 2028 Speculation

Columbia University in June joined seven other Ivy League institutions in going away from test-optional policies, announcing it would reinstate standardized testing requirements for undergraduate applicants starting next year, according to HigherEdDive.

Berkeley did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Concerns about coddled or underprepared students at elite schools are hardly exclusive to California.

Fox News Digital reported last week that freshmen at the University of Michigan next year will get a semester-long break from having letter grades appear on their transcripts as school officials look for new ways to combat the "mental health crisis" affecting higher education.

title: He’s Probably California’s Next Governor — So Why Does No One Know What He Thinks?
description: The enigma of Xavier Becerra.
fullText:
SACRAMENTO — Xavier Becerra is keeping people guessing.

The presumptive next leader of California traced a circuitous path through the state's most chaotic governor race in a generation. He was not the first or second or even third or fourth choice of most Democratic kingmakers, prevailing over a fractured field after better-positioned candidates either passed on running (Kamala Harris, Alex Padilla) or imploded (Eric Swalwell). Becerra effectively punched his ticket to lead America's largest state — a progressive bastion, a Democratic bellwether and a national launching pad — by winning 28 percent of primary voters.

Now, as Sacramento prepares for Becerra's all but inevitable ascension, the elected officials, lobbyists, and corporate and labor leaders who shape policy in one of the nation's most consequential capitals are grappling with a contradiction: Despite Becerra's decades in public service, no one seems to be quite sure what he'll do with the biggest job of his career. And the ambiguity seems to be by design.

"I can make some really big promises. But that doesn't get us anywhere — it may get us elected, but I would prefer not to run on inflated promises that I can't deliver on," Becerra told POLITICO this week, subsequently telling reporters his caution was a product of hard-learned experience, like his time helping to lead the White House's response to the Covid-19 pandemic: "When I was dealing with Covid, I could not say 'I'm going to get you all the ventilators you need,' because I didn't want people to say — 'you promised them, (and) because you didn't bring them, these people died."

He remains something of a cipher, even to some of California's most attentive political observers, despite having served at virtually every level of government. He rose from the state legislature to Congress to statewide office to a cabinet position in President Joe Biden's administration leading the Health and Human Services Agency.

But none of those roles carry the same weight as the governor's office, both as a matter of policy impact and given the power California governors have to define the Democratic Party. Becerra will almost certainly become a prominent target for President Donald Trump and national Republicans who need no encouragement to vilify California Democrats.

Conversely, he can help chart Democrats' course as disaffected voters say they crave bold, authentic leaders. Becerra will lead a fall campaign against a Republican-backed voter ID ballot initiative, allowing him to step into the anti-Trump crusader role that Gov. Gavin Newsom has enthusiastically embraced.

As for policy, while Becerra has offered a few concrete proposals, like freezing insurance rates, offering a block of free electricity, and identifying "shovel-ready" housing projects, he prevailed in the primary by running as a steady hand for an era of budget deficits and political upheaval. The candidate of big swings was Becerra's chief rival, billionaire Tom Steyer, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars to seize the progressive lane and vowed to institute single-payer health care, tax billionaires and shatter utility monopolies.

"I think in some ways, Becerra has the freedom to be able to put his plan together on his timeline," said Amanda Renteria, who was a senior aide to Becerra when he was attorney general. "There wasn't some big expectation when he was in the election cycle to have big, bombastic promises in the sort of Mamdani fashion — that's not how he rolls. He ran on being thoughtful and experienced."

Becerra wants California to be more affordable. He wants to make health care universally accessible, as befits a former health and human services secretary who oversaw a massive expansion in insurance coverage. He abhors Trump, as you'd expect from a former California attorney general who prolifically sued him.

Fusing those two themes, he said last week that he intends to restore health insurance to the millions of Californians poised to lose it because of Trump's policies — a monumental undertaking that he hasn't quite explained how he'd achieve.

Similarly, Sacramento is still hazy on the details of how Becerra would govern after his unexpectedly meteoric rise to the top of the governor's race. Insiders are asking information about how to get in touch with Becerra and trading rumors about who he might hire.

One prominent lobbyist, who insisted on anonymity to convey sensitive dynamics, likened the unsettled state of affairs to "walking into a final exam and realizing you studied the wrong material."

"So we are all trying to get through multiple choice questions by eliminating obviously wrong answers and then making educated guesses," the lobbyist said in a text message.

When he is asked about his plans, Becerra falls back on a ready refrain: look at my record. Want to know how he'll approach climate change after he was pilloried for receiving Chevron money and saying California needs the oil giant? Research his lawsuits against fossil fuel companies. In response to an inquiry for this story, a spokesman pointed to his past statements and actions.

But he's also looking ahead. Becerra has been taking meetings with lobbying firms, industry associations, labor groups and tech titans. He is studying up on issues like California's budget crunch and the impact of steep federal cuts leveled by HR1, working with a small and now highly in-demand coterie of advisers.

That partially reflects Becerra's longstanding approach to politics. The Stanford-educated lawyer prefers to rigorously study issues and run exhaustively through the pros and cons with his team. Once he arrives at his decision, he can be immovable.

"There's not going to be a lot of hyperbolic pronouncements. There's not going to be a lot of rhetorically pushing the envelope," said Roger Salazar, a political consultant who has known Becerra for years and worked for his attorney general campaign. "That's just not who Xavier is. He's a steady person who takes his time to formulate policies and then sticks to them."

Some players — particularly those who did not support Becerra — have a less charitable interpretation. A methodical approach can look plodding or equivocal, ill-suited to a moment when California is facing converging challenges like climate change, pervasive homelessness, a reeling insurance market and periodic population loss.

Becerra has been dogged by accusations from fellow Biden alumni that he was ill-prepared for his role as health and human services secretary and slow to respond to crises like a surge of unaccompanied minors at the southern border. While Becerra and allies like former Biden chief of staff Ron Klain have dismissed those critiquesas unfounded or uninformed, they have nevertheless circulated in Sacramento.

One interest group leader, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, met with Becerra hoping to get specifics and instead received vague assurances about bringing people to the table — a not uncommon takeaway as Becerra makes the rounds.

"We haven't heard a vision from him on what his goals are for the state of California," the person said. "It was a lot of those phrases but a lack of specificity and substance on what he plans to do."

Every governor is measured against their predecessors. Becerra presents a marked contrast to the outsize personalities he will likely follow into office: Arnold Schwarzenegger's global starpower, Jerry Brown's unrivaled experience and relentless focus on a small handful of issues, Gavin Newsom's oozing ambition and propensity for headline-grabbing proposals.

He also won a very different kind of election. Unlike 2018, when Newsom was the clear candidate to beat and secured support from traditional powers like organized labor, Becerra spent much of the race languishing in the lower tier of candidates before rocketing to the top of the field after Swalwell''s departure created a vacuum.

That precipitous rise meant Becerra faced less scrutiny than a candidate who spends months as the frontrunner. Moneyed interests spent much of their resources on thwarting Steyer, casting Becerra in the role of the reasonable alternative.

And even though Becerra eventually emerged as the candidate to beat, he did so without locking down the sole endorsements of Democratic allies — in particular organized labor groups like the California Teachers Association and SEIU California, an influential collection of service unions — who are usually indispensable for statewide candidates.

Becerra and his team are well aware that he was not the favorite. But with that snub comes a form of freedom. Unbound by litmus tests or policy pledges, Becerra could have more room to maneuver — and even less incentive to squander that runway by committing to an extensive policy agenda.

"It gives him a lot of leeway that I don't think most governors have had — even those who have won with big mandates," said a second interest group official, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about private dynamics. "Nobody thought he was going to win, so no one was putting him through the ringer on this stuff, so now he has a great opportunity to say: 'I'm not beholden to anyone. What do I want to do with this?'"

Becerra has kept a relatively low public profile since winning the primary — a conspicuous contrast with his Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, who has maintained a steady stream of events and new proposals as he seeks to make up ground. Becerra has begun to pivot toward the general election, delving into ballot politics by spearheading an anti-voter ID push as a way of protecting California against Trumpism — a winning strategy for governors in a state where anti-MAGA animus abounds.

Despite growing up in Sacramento, Becerra is not seen as a creature of the state capital. The single term he spent in the state Assembly and his four years as attorney general are dwarfed by the decades he spent in Washington, first in Congress — where he became close to Rep. Nancy Pelosi — and then in the Biden administration.

That magnifies the importance of his impending staffing decisions. Becerra is broadly known to be especially reliant on his closest aides. But his former chief of staff recently pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges — Becerra has not been implicated in any wrongdoing and has forcefully pushed back on efforts to do so — creating more uncertainty about who he might hire.

The team currently surrounding him includes longtime staffers and more recent additions with links to Newsom's orbit, including Lindsey Cobia and Courtni Pugh — two Newsom-world veterans who came onto the Becerra campaign in the later stages — and policy adviser Nicole Elliott, who oversaw cannabis regulation in the Newsom administration and is married to inner-circle Newsom loyalist Jason Elliott.

The mix of familiar and new faces has fueled more speculation about a larger shift underway. Newsom has towered over the state's politics for nearly a decade, trumpeting California as a national model for Democrats and, in the process, refining the public conception of what California represents. The state's size and industrial might give it tremendous sway over national politics and commerce.

As Newsom prepares to conclude his Sacramento era and looks ahead to a likely presidential campaign, California is trying to figure out if Becerra represents more of the same or a shift to something new.

For now, Becerra occupies an interstitial space. A November victory is basically a foregone conclusion, but he still has a race to run — raising money for a fall campaign that re-introduces him to voters. At the same time,he has to both show deference to Newsom while preparing to succeed him.

There hasn't been any formal contact between Becerra's team and the Newsom administration, according to people familiar with discussions, although the two principals met at a San Francisco restaurant soon after Becerra's primary victory.

But a change is coming. And Newsom's team is preparing papers and memos to both brief his successor and make the case for preserving some of the governor's policies.

"There's a lot of planning to make sure the next governor has a seamless transition, from the budget announcement in January to maintaining existing programs to the thousands of new appointments he'll have to make," Newsom spokesperson Bob Salladay said in a text message. "Obviously, the next Governor will have his own priorities, but we're going to lay out in detail everything Governor Newsom has been working on, and what we feel needs to be protected and managed."

Both politicians have reasons to think beyond November. Becerra is preparing for the possibility that he'll soon oversee the world's fifth-largest economy. Newsom is looking to shape what comes after his governorship by smoothing the handoff and laying out his priorities.

Newsom's office declined to elaborate on which initiatives he'd most want Becerra to preserve. But Becerra has offered some clues about what he might do.

He has said he will maintain Newsom's moratorium on the death penalty while breaking with the governor on other fronts. Becerra has pledged to restore health coverage for undocumented immigrants that Newsom pared back and indicated he would reverse a Department of Motor Vehicle regulation allowing autonomous trucks without human drivers on board — a departure from Newsom's history of thwarting labor's push to limit self-driving vehicles. He initially raised doubts about Newsom's order banning sales of new gas-powered vehicles in 2035 before saying on Tuesday he believed it was achievable.

And Newsom has ensured that a major test will land on Becerra's agenda in the first few months of his term. For most of his time in office Newsom, a relative economic moderate, resisted raising taxes. Then, under pressure to find more revenue, Newsom this year signed legislation requiring California to develop a plan for a labor priority: charging corporations whose employees earn low enough wages that they qualify for public benefits.

Becerra has said he supports the policy and suggested it could pay for his goal of keeping Californians insured — potentially delivering a landmark win for some of the same labor unions that did not support him until it was clear he would win. But it would also antagonize business groups like the California Chamber of Commerce, which broke with longstanding practice by endorsing Becerra after having strenuously opposed Steyer.

And it would require securing two-thirds votes for higher taxes from the legislature — never an easy task, despite Democrats' overwhelming margins in Sacramento, and one that would serve as an early gauge of his relationship with lawmakers who are still assessing their likely next governor.

So will he do it? The man poised to be one of Becerra's key allies in Sacramento couldn't say.

Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas forged a relationship with Becerra years ago. Rivas was a newly elected lawmaker from an obscure coastal enclave who was surprised to get an encouraging call from the attorney general of California. Nearly a decade later, Rivas emerged as one of Becerra's more prominent endorsers, rallying his caucus at the moment when Becerra needed to cement his nascent frontrunner status. Rivas will now devote some of his fall to campaigning with Becerra against a voter ID ballot initiative.

But as for what Becerra will do if he's elected, Rivas said he "can't say for certain he's going to focus on issue X, A, B or C." Nevertheless, Rivas said he was confident his old friend was "going to have an ambitious plan and an agenda" — even if it's not his style to trumpet that vision.

"He doesn't wake up every morning thinking how he can make headlines or be on the front page of our newspapers," Rivas said. "He's someone that doesn't ever have to speak the loudest, but you can'' mistake that as being passive. That's not who Xavier is. He's intensely competitive, he's extremely persistent and he's certainly planning for the future."

title: Republicans won the redistricting competition. Don't tell that to this California congressman
description: One thing Anne Smull, a retired feedstore owner, was looking forward to on Election Day was voting for the man who currently represents her in Congress, conservative Rep. Kevin Kiley.  During a recent...
fullText:
LINCOLN, Calif. (AP) — One thing Anne Smull, a retired feedstore owner, was looking forward to on Election Day was voting for the man who currently represents her in Congress, conservative Rep. Kevin Kiley. Now she can't.

That's because California Democrats sliced Kiley's district six ways as payback for Republican redistricting in Texas and elsewhere. The chunk of the district that Smull, who identifies as a conservative, lives in is now grafted onto an overwhelmingly Democratic seat based in the state's wine country.

During a recent lunch at a cafe in Lincoln, a onetime agricultural town that has morphed into a bedroom community on the edge of Sacramento's exurban sprawl, Smull was heartbroken to hear she can no longer vote for Kiley.

"He believes in the same things I do," Smull said. "It feels sneaky and underhanded."

Democratic voters in several other states know how Smull feels.

President Donald Trump last year told GOP-controlled states to redraw their maps before this year's midterm elections to increase the number of winnable seats for Republicans in order to help the party hold onto the U.S. House. The effort was turbocharged by a U.S. Supreme Court decision this spring that neutralized a key provision of the Voting Rights Act and cleared the way for Republicans to redraw more seats across the South that had elected Black Democrats.

Democratic-leaning and heavily minority communities from Texas to Tennessee have been split into multiple congressional districts that dilute the Democratic vote by stretching deep into conservative areas.

In the future, it is likely that more Republican voters in other states will go through what Smull and other conservatives in Northern California are facing. Democrats in Maryland, New York, Illinois and other strongholds have pledged to retaliate in time for the 2028 elections and split Republican-leaning districts the way their California counterparts did Kiley's.

Democrats have been hindered nationally by stricter rules against partisan line-drawing in their states, but California showed a way around that. California Democrats won voter approval last year to redraw the state's congressional map, originally made by an independent commission, and formed five new Democratic-leaning seats.

Kiley's is one of them. The reworked political lines led the two-term congressman to leave the Republican Party and run as an independent in the slightly Democratic-leaning district that now includes his home.

He spoke out against partisan gerrymandering, even unsuccessfully trying to force the Republican-led House to allow a vote on a bill to ban mid-decade redistricting.

"We've seen partisan divisions really spin out of control in really harmful ways, and I think exhibit number one is the redistricting wars," Kiley recently told a group of voters in the suburb of Citrus Heights.

Democrats contend Kiley's party switch is purely a political trick to survive in a more liberal district. They note he still caucuses with House Republicans, has voted for many of the GOP's priorities, including Trump's sweeping budget and tax cut bill last year, and that political organizations run by House Republicans are spending money to back his reelection.

Even some of Kiley's supporters think the election was a factor in the congressman's decision to become an independent.

"My original thinking was he did it because of redistricting — maybe it'd help him get reelected," said John Coburn, a 68-year-old retired business owner, at the Citrus Heights event.

Coburn is furious at the Democrats' redistricting and hopes Kiley wins. Coburn does not care that they did it in retaliation for Texas, where Republicans at Trump's directive revised that state's map to carve out up to five new winnable conservative seats.

"I don't care about Texas, I live in California," Coburn said, adding that "40% of the state is Republican, and we have zero voice. Zero. It's not how our Founding Fathers intended."

In an interview, Kiley said his switch to independent was no political gambit. If he wanted to stay in the House, he argued, he could have had an easier time staying in the GOP, moving to a more conservative district that included parts of his old one and running in a Republican primary there.

"I could have gone there and run and played the same game these other politicians are playing," he said.

Kiley said he is caucusing with Republicans to avoid losing his seats on committees and that in the next Congress he will try to change rules so independent members do not lose committee seats because they do not caucus with one of the two major parties.

Among his backers, he noted, is onetime Democratic presidential hopeful Andrew Yang, a former technology entrepreneur who co-founded a centrist party for independents.

The Democrat running against Kiley, former state Sen. Richard Pan, scoffs at his rival's newfound independent status.

"He was a MAGA champion when he first ran for Congress, and now he's trying to say 'I'm not,'" Pan told a crowd at a senior community in Roseville, referring to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.

Earlier that day, Pan swung by the Placer County Democratic Party office, tucked away on the second story of a brick shopping arcade in Lincoln's compact downtown.

Placer is a Republican county that stretches from the Sacramento suburbs to the northwestern shores of Lake Tahoe. The entire county is in Kiley's current district, but it will be divided among three districts in the new map.

Kathleen Crawford, chair of the county Democratic Party, was enthusiastic about the county getting carved up.

"It's worth it, because we have an opportunity to get Democratic representation, which has been missing from our county," Crawford said. "I've been here 15 years, and this is my first real opportunity to elect a Democrat."

Lincoln's downtown is flanked by fruit, vegetable and flower farms, as well as new subdivisions. The community and its neighboring suburbs have become a destination for people fleeing the San Francisco Bay Area's housing prices. That has helped change the once solidly conservative area into a political battleground where skilled mapmakers can draw winnable seats for Democrats.

Ed Church, a 61-year-old risk manager, was eating lunch at Simple Pleasures cafe in Lincoln when he contemplated Kiley's shift. A Democrat, Church has not been a Kiley fan and he was bemused by the congressman's move.

"If that's how he'd been initially and not so MAGA, I probably could have supported him," Church said of Kiley's independent status. Now Church, as a Lincoln resident, is in a purely Democratic district and will not have a say in Kiley's fate in November. His main criteria in the election will be "who's going to stand up to Trump?"

Across the street at a gun store, Wesley Johnson, 43, who considers himself a conservative independent, said he was dispirited by the state's redistricting.

"I feel Northern California is not represented fairly," Johnson said. "San Francisco, Sacramento and Los Angeles control everything."

He acknowledged Republicans were doing the same thing in states they controlled and said he did not know how it could stop.

"You're just cutting out the little people," Johnson said.

title: Pallister stuns Ledecky in Pan Pacs 800m free as two world records carry Douglass to gold
description: Australian Lani Pallister dealt US great Katie Ledecky her first 800m freestyle defeat in a major international meet on Saturday, beating her one-time idol at the Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California.Canadian Summer McIntosh did beat Ledecky in the 800m free at a minor domestic meeting in Florida in February of 2024.
fullText:
Australian Lani Pallister dealt US great Katie Ledecky her first 800m freestyle defeat in a major international meet on Saturday, beating her one-time idol at the Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California.

Pallister led wire-to-wire on the way to victory in 8min 06.10sec and Ledecky's desperate late charge wasn't enough as she finished second in 8:07.26.

It was a stunning result on the final day of Pan Pacs action that saw American Kate Douglass break the 50m freestyle world record twice on the way to gold and earn 200m breaststroke silver and medley relay gold as well.

Ledecky has dominated the 800m since she won Olympic gold in 2012 as a 15-year-old, winning 13 international golds since then. That includes four Olympic gold medals and seven world titles in the event.

Canadian Summer McIntosh did beat Ledecky in the 800m free at a minor domestic meeting in Florida in February of 2024.

But world record-holder Ledecky maintained her hold on the event with a razor-thin victory over Pallister and McIntosh in a World Championships thriller last year in Singapore, where Ledecky said her rule as younger swimmers began closing in was "I don't lose 800s."

Pallister, who claimed her first career win over Ledecky in the 400m free earlier this week before finishing second behind her in the 1,500m, showed that rule can be broken as the 29-year-old American looks to adding to her collection of nine Olympic gold medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The Australian punched the water in delight and got a hug across the lane rope from Ledecky.

"Katie is such a dominant force," said Pallister, who finished the week with gold in the 200, 400 and 800m free and the 4x200m free relay.

"Without her, we wouldn't have women's distance swimming in the place we're at at the moment.

"To be part of that story at the moment (it's) pretty much all because we get to chase Katie."

Douglass, meanwhile, firmly established herself as the one to chase in the 50m free, winning the final in a devastating 23.19sec.

That sliced three-tenths of a second off the world record of 23.49sec she set hours earlier and saw her finish a whopping 55-hundredths of a second ahead of US teammate Gretchen Walsh.

Walsh had set a world record of 23.55 on June 28 in Rome -- where she broke the world mark Douglass had set on June 19.

Australia's reigning world champion Meg Harris took bronze in 23.89.

Douglass returned less than half an hour later to claim silver in the 200m breaststroke won by Canadian Alexanne LePage in 2:21.73.

Douglass capped her night swimming the freestyle anchor leg for the US 4x100 medley relay team that took gold in 3:50.43, 4.66sec ahead of Australia.

Australian Jamie Jack won the men's 50m free in 21.35sec and Zac Stubblety-Cook rallied from fourth at the final turn to win the men's 200m breaststroke in 2:08.09 and give Australia another gold in the four-day meeting of top swimmers from non-European countries.

- More McIntosh disappointment -

Chinese Olympian Yu Yiting started the night with an upset of world record-holder Summer McIntosh in the 200m medley, leading most of the way and holding off the Canadian's charge on the final freestyle leg to win in 2:07.45.

McIntosh, the reigning world and Olympic champion, touched in 2:07.47.

It was another disappointment for McIntosh in a meet that included 400m medley gold but only silver in the 200m free and a failure to make the championship final in the 400m free.

Japan's Tomoyuki Matsushita completed a men's medley double with a 200m victory in 1:56.02.

Sam Short clocked an Australian record of 14:33.97 to add 1,500m freestyle to his 400m and 800m gold.

Short, who pulled off the same treble at the Commonwealth Games, finished 8.62sec in front of Japan's Kazushi Imafuku and said he was inspired by the world record of 14:26.79 set by Germany's Johannes Liebmann at the European Championships in Paris on Saturday.

American Bobby Finke, the two-time Olympic gold medallist whose world mark was broken by Liebmann, was third in 14:44.26.

title: Liebmann and Douglass set world records on same day
description: Germany's Johannes Liebmann and American Kate Douglass set swimming world records on Saturday, dazzling crowds at events in Paris and California.
fullText:
Germany's Johannes Liebmann and American Kate Douglass set swimming world records on Saturday, dazzling at events held in Paris and California.

Liebmann, 19, knocked nearly four seconds off the men's 1500m freestyle record as he claimed his first international gold medal at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.

He completed the distance in 14 minutes 26.79 seconds - 3.88secs faster than the previous record which was set by American Bobby Finke at the 2024 Olympics, also held in the French capital.

Liebmann became the first swimmer to go under 14:30 for the distance as he slashed the most time off the record since Australia's Grant Hackett in 2001.

Three-time Olympic champion Hackett took more than seven seconds off when he swam 14:34.56 - a record which stood for 10 years.

Douglass broke the women's 50m freestyle record for the second time this summer, achieving her feat in California during heats at the Pan Pacific Championships.

The two-time Olympic champion, 24, clocked 23.49secs to regain the record from Gretchen Walsh.

Douglass swam 23.59 in June before compatriot Walsh lowered the mark to 23.55 nine days later.

fullText:
World record-holder Summer McIntosh failed to qualify for the 400m freestyle final at the Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California, on Friday, slumping to the ninth-quickest time in the heats.

The 19-year-old Canadian sensation, who won three gold medals at the Paris Olympics, clocked 4min 08.56sec -- more than 14 seconds outside the world record she set last year before going on to win the world title in Singapore.

McIntosh had been expected to figure in a three-way battle for the Pan Pacs crown with US freestyle great Katie Ledecky and Australian Lani Pallister.

Ledecky led the way into Friday night's final with a time of 4:03.48 and Pallister, who won the 200m free and took silver behind Ledecky in the 1,500m on Wednesday, was fourth-quickest.

The competition that brings together top swimmers from non-European countries has been a mixed bag for McIntosh.

After dropping one of her signature events, the 200m butterfly, to focus on the 200m free she finished runner-up to Pallister. She went on to win the 400m individual medley on Thursday, shattering the championship record but saying she was disappointed in her time of 4:28.01, which was more than four seconds slower than her world mark.

title: Despite emergency appeal to Supreme Court, Bruce the dog euthanized in California
description: The dog was deemed "vicious" after multiple biting incidents.
fullText:
Despite a last-minute appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, a 3-year-old 100-pound Great Pyrenees/German Shepherd mix named Bruce, who had been deemed legally "vicious," was euthanized in California on Wednesday, according to the lawyer for an animal rescue center that had sued to stop the move.

The case involving the imminent execution of a personal pet was a highly unusual, if not unprecedented, appeal to reach the court's emergency docket, which typically sees eleventh-hour pleas in capital cases and urgent disputes over government policy.

The dog was euthanized by Ventura County Animal Services (VCAS) before Justice Elena Kagan, who oversees emergency applications in the Ninth Circuit, could weigh in, attorney Dan Bolton confirmed to ABC News.

'Profoundly corrupt': Trump sued in federal court over selling early access to Truth Social posts

Bolton represents the Santa Paula Animal Rescue Center (SPAR), which had overseen the original adoption of the dog and claimed a contractual interest in its wellbeing.

The animal rescue sought to block the euthanasia mandated by local officials and was joined by the dog's owner, Claire Birgy. The legal saga drew national attention.

Bolton said the local case presented, in his view, important constitutional questions on standing.

Lower courts had tossed out the last-ditch appeals to save Bruce by concluding the animal rescue lacked a concrete interest in the dog's survival sufficient to challenge the dangerousness finding by local authorities.

Federal court blocks another part of Trump mail-in voting executive order

In April, a judge determined Bruce was a "vicious dog" and ordered him euthanized after finding he posed a threat to the public after multiple "vicious" biting incidents.

On its website, Ventura County Animal Services described the incidents and released graphic photos of some of the bite wounds. In one case, in February 2024, VCAS said a male minor was bitten on the lips while walking past Bruce "resulting in severe disfiguring lacerations."

In another incident, from September 2025, a man walking past Bruce, who was tied to a pole outside a CVS, was attacked, resulting in "multiple bite wounds to the knee, chest, and forearm and required sutures," according to VCAS.

In November, a woman was walking in her apartment complex when she was walking past the dog and was bitten on the arm, later requiring surgery and skin grafts, according to VCAS.

Bruce was initially ordered to be euthanized no later than May 15, but that was temporarily delayed by a stay issued by a federal court. The stay was lifted earlier this month.

In a statement on Tuesday, Ventura County Animal Services said: "Decisions involving the humane euthanasia of an animal are difficult and complex.  They require us to balance compassion for animals with our responsibility to protect people and ensure public safety.  Dog bite cases are challenging, and we recognize the strong emotions they can generate within our community."

title: Why Utah commit Dillon Sykes moved to Beehive State ahead of senior season
description: Elite receiver Dillon Sykes traded California for Lone Peak High to master his transition, build local bonds, and immerse himself in Salt Lake City’s culture before joining the Utes.
fullText:
Utah Utes football commit Dillon Sykes is officially leaving home.

The elite 6-foot-5 wide receiver has made the move from California to the Beehive State and will spend his senior season at Lone Peak High School before enrolling early at the University of Utah.

A lot of recruits commit to a school.

Not many move to that state nearly a year before they ever step on campus for their freshman year.

That's exactly what Sykes has done.

For Dillon, the move wasn't about leaving California behind. It was about getting a head start on the next chapter of his life and making the transition into Utah's program as smooth as possible.

Before the move, Sykes told me the decision came down to getting closer to the program, the coaching staff and the place he'll call home over the next several years.

"California is great. I love it here," Sykes said. "I appreciate everybody that's helped me here, but really it's just to get closer to the program, to the coaches, to everybody and make the adjustment easier."

California is where Sykes grew into one of Utah's top recruiting priorities. It's where he earned his first Power Four offer from the Utes and built the relationships that eventually led to his commitment.

Now, he's beginning the next step.

Before arriving in Utah, Sykes said he wanted the opportunity to become more familiar with both the state and the people around the program before officially becoming a college player.

"I just want to get more used to Utah, the state I'm going to be in for three, four, five years," Sykes said. "I want to see what they have to offer as a state. I really just want to see more, do more out there, get more involved."

The move also allows Sykes to spend his senior year around the program instead of following it from hundreds of miles away.

He'll be able to attend games at Rice-Eccles Stadium, continue building relationships with the coaching staff and play his final high school season just a short drive from Salt Lake City.

"I can go to the games more," Sykes said. "I heard the games are a great environment, and the coaches can come see me at any time. Every Friday night, wherever I am, I shouldn't be too far from Salt Lake."

"They can come see me. I can go see them and just continue to build the relationship and make this transition easier."

That relationship has always been one of the biggest reasons Utah separated itself.

The Utes were there early in Sykes' recruitment, and that held a lot of weight. Wide receivers coach Chad Bumphis believed in him, Morgan Scalley's vision connected with him, and the staff consistently made him feel like more than just another recruit.

When Sykes discussed the possibility of moving to Utah with the coaching staff, they fully supported the idea.

"They talked to me about it," Sykes said. "They said if I move out there, they would love it regardless of where I go. I can come see them. They can come see me. It'll just be an easier transition, and I can get to know everybody better."

There was also a little rivalry talk mixed into the conversations.

"They wanted me to stay away from the other team in Utah, so they wanted me to be closer to Salt Lake," Sykes said.

Dillon plans to graduate early, allowing him to make a short move north to campus once his high school career ends.

"As soon as I graduate high school, because I'll be an early grad, I'll probably just move 30 or 40 minutes away from where I was," Sykes said. "It's not too much of a big deal to me."

For Utah, the move is another example of just how invested Sykes is in the program.

The Utes found Dillon early, built genuine relationships, and ultimately earned his commitment after his official visit.

Now, before he has even signed his National Letter of Intent or stepped on campus as a student-athlete, Sykes has already made Utah home.

It's not something many recruits do.

But it says everything about how committed Dillon Sykes is to the future he's building with the Utes and is already on track to be a future Utah great.

title: The 25 best state universities in the US, ranked
description: The ranking of the 25 best public schools in the US includes seven in California.
fullText:
US News & World Report ranks the best universities across the US every year.

While many of the top schools are private, every state in the union has its own public system.

We used US News' ranking to compile a list of the 25 best public schools.

This back-to-school season, the cost and value of higher education are top of mind.

In a time when going to college can put you in hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and as more tech moguls share that they skipped university altogether, it could be worth considering a public school.

Every state has some sort of public school system, though they're not all created equal. Just as private schools have the Ivy League, some state schools stand above the rest — Forbes now releases its own list of "Public Ivies" each year.

Public schools are also generally cheaper than private schools, especially if you stay in-state. But even paying out-of-state tuition at some public schools can cost half as much as the most expensive colleges charge.

We used US News & World Report's ranking of best national universities to identify the top 25 public schools in the country. The list does not include liberal arts colleges focused on undergraduate education or regional universities with limited doctoral programs, although those are typically private schools.

Its ranking evaluated 434 US colleges across multiple metrics, including graduation rates, debt loads, average salaries, and admissions rates, among others, using data reported by schools and third-party sources.

College rankings have faced scrutiny over the years, with critics of US News & World Report's lists arguing that they can pressure schools to perform well on certain metrics to boost their standing. Skeptics have also questioned the ranking methodology, saying it may fail to capture key, less quantifiable factors that add to a school's quality.

US News has defended the rankings as a helpful resource, while admitting comparing colleges "can be challenging," and the lists "don't capture every nuance."

"But we reject our critics' paternalistic view that students are somehow incapable of discerning for themselves from this information which school is the best fit," US News & World Report executive chairman and CEO Eric Gertler wrote in 2023 for the Wall Street Journal.

Here are the 25 best public universities across the US.

25. University of California, Merced

UC Merced, which opened in 2005, is the newest school in the UC system. It's around 80 miles west of Yosemite National Park and has an enrollment of around 9,000 students, including undergraduates and graduates.

It's a top performer in US News' social mobility ranking, which means the university admits a large number of economically disadvantaged students and distributes Pell Grants to help them afford higher education.

21 (tie). Florida State University

Florida State University, located in Tallahassee, Florida's capital city, was founded in 1851. It has an enrollment of about 33,000 undergraduate students.

FSU is known as the home of the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, the only magnet-powered lab in the country and one of just 12 in the world.

Texas A&M is located in College Station, about 90 miles northwest of Houston, and was founded in 1876, 150 years ago this year. It has an enrollment of 61,000 undergraduate students.

Aside from its academics, Texas A&M is also known for its close ties to President George H. W. Bush. His presidential library is located on campus, and the school of government and public service is named after him. His gravesite is also on campus, near his library.

The town of Blacksburg is home to Virginia Tech, or the Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, founded in 1872.

Virginia Tech has about 31,000 undergraduate students enrolled. It ranks No. 6 for the best industrial/manufacturing engineering program.

21 (tie). College of William & Mary

The second school on this list (but not the last) located in Virginia is the College of William & Mary, which is in Williamsburg. It's named for King William III and Queen Mary II, who ruled England from 1689 to 1702.

The college itself was founded in 1693, making it the second-oldest college in the US. About 7,000 undergraduates are enrolled.

It ranked highly for its commitment to teaching undergrads rather than focusing on graduate-level research.

Purdue is located in West Lafayette, Indiana, about 65 miles northwest of Indianapolis, with about 45,000 undergraduates calling this campus home. It was founded in 1869.

Purdue is famously called the "Cradle of Astronauts," as 30 astronauts across NASA history have been Purdue alums, including Neil Armstrong.

19 (tie). University of Georgia

UGA, located in Athens, was chartered by the state in 1785, making it the oldest state-chartered university in the US.

It has an enrollment of about 32,000 undergraduate students.

Per US News, UGA has the No. 1 insurance program in the country, which was founded in 1965.

16 (tie). Rutgers University — New Brunswick

Rutgers has three campuses across New Jersey, but the biggest, located in New Brunswick, was ruled its best. It was founded in 1766 as Queen's College, before getting renamed Rutgers in 1825.

Approximately 38,000 undergraduates are enrolled at the New Brunswick campus.

16 (tie). University of Washington

Founded in 1861, the University of Washington is located in the middle of Seattle and has an undergraduate enrollment of about 41,000 students.

UW has strong nursing and computer science programs, both cracking US News' top 10 lists.

16 (tie). University of Maryland, College Park

The College Park campus is the largest in the UMD system, with about 31,000 undergraduate students. It was founded in 1856.

College Park is just over 8 miles from downtown Washington, DC, and 30 miles from Baltimore, making it a relatively easy commute to either city.

UMD's cybersecurity program ranks at No. 9.

The Ohio State University, or OSU, has an undergraduate enrollment of about 47,000 students. Founded in 1870, it's located in northern Columbus, the Buckeye State's capital.

OSU has a well-regarded nursing program (No. 4), accounting program (No. 12), and supply chain/logistics program (No. 5).

14. University of California, Santa Barbara

Nearly 24,000 undergraduates call UCSB, founded in 1909, home.

Much can be said about UCSB's strong academics, but it's probably most famous for its proximity to the beach, making it a dream school for aspiring surfers everywhere.

12 (tie). University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

About 140 miles southwest of Chicago, you'll find the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the flagship school of the UI system. It was founded in 1867 and has an undergrad population of 37,000.

UIUC — or, according to a recent branding shift, Illinois — was ranked fifth overall in the nation for its school of engineering, which was founded in 1868, making it one of the oldest schools at the university.

12 (tie). University of Wisconsin — Madison

UW-Madison's 939-acre campus, located in the heart of Madison, is home to 39,000 undergraduate students.

Founded in 1848, it's ranked in the top 10 for nursing, insurance, marketing, real estate, and computer systems.

9 (tie). Georgia Institute of Technology

The second Georgia university on the list is located a mile from downtown Atlanta. Georgia Tech was founded in 1885 and has an undergraduate population of about 20,000.

It was ranked the third-most innovative school, behind MIT and Arizona State.

9 (tie). University of California, Davis

Fun fact: UC Davis is the northernmost undergraduate campus in the University of California system, above both San Francisco and Berkeley.

It was founded in 1905 and has roughly 32,000 undergraduates.

UC Davis is tied for No. 2 among universities with the best biological/agricultural engineering programs.

9 (tie). University of California, Irvine

UC Davis is tied with another California school: UC Irvine, located in Orange County, with an undergraduate population of 30,000.

The school was founded in 1965 and is best-known for its STEM programs. That, and its mascot, the anteater.

Gainesville is home to the University of Florida, founded in 1853. It's in northern Florida, roughly 110 miles northwest of Orlando.

There are about 36,000 undergraduate Gators running around the 2,000-acre grounds — and they're (probably) all powered by Gatorade, the famed sports drink that was created right there on campus by researchers looking to help athletes replenish their electrolytes and stay hydrated.

7 (tie). University of Texas at Austin

UT Austin, founded in 1883, takes up a big chunk of Texas' capital city — in fact, it's just a 15-minute walk from campus to see the Lone Star State's statehouse. It has 43,000 undergraduates.

Many UT programs are world-renowned, but the Moody College of Communication is among its most famous.

6. University of California, San Diego

From the northernmost UC school to the southernmost — UC San Diego, established in 1960, is approximately 30 minutes from the California/Mexico border.

The university, which has 35,000 undergraduate students, is known for its strong engineering and biotechnology programs.

4 (tie). University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

UNC-Chapel Hill, located less than 30 miles west of Raleigh, was founded in 1789 and has an undergraduate population of 21,000.

Besides its famed NCAA basketball team, Chapel Hill has a top 10 business school and a top five nursing school.

4 (tie). University of Virginia

The University of Virginia, or UVA, was founded in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 1819. It has about 18,000 undergraduate students.

In addition to its strong undergraduate programs, the UVA School of Law is the No. 4 law school in the nation, according to US US News.

The University of Michigan, known colloquially as "Michigan," was founded in Ann Arbor in 1817, which is about 40 miles west of Detroit.

Michigan has an undergraduate population of 34,000 students. It's best known for the Ross School of Business, which ranks No. 13 among full-time MBA programs in the US.

2. University of California, Los Angeles

UCLA, founded in 1919 and located in the Westwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, is one of the biggest universities in the UC system, with 33,000 undergraduates and a well-regarded medical school, law school, and public health master's program.

It also has just a 9% acceptance rate, making it a highly sought-after acceptance letter.

1. University of California, Berkeley

UC Berkeley (or simply Cal) was named by US News & World Report as the best public school in the US. Founded in 1868, it is the oldest university in the University of California system.

Its 33,000 undergraduate students call the Bay Area home, and the university has top-five biomedical, chemical, civil, computer, electrical, environmental, industrial/manufacturing, materials, and mechanical engineering programs.

Water systems in smaller communities depend on internet-connected automated systems, with many lacking the resources to provide adequate security. In response to the attacks, a bipartisan group of lawmakers last week urged the restoration of federal funding for Department of Homeland Security programs designed to coordinate multi-state cybersecurity efforts.

Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, in a statement to The Times, said that there is no evidence that California water systems were among those targeted in the recent spate of attacks. However, the governor’s office noted that state-by-state cybersecurity efforts are less effective than a coordinated federal response.

title: Many immigrants face deportation without a lawyer at their side in court. This program tries to help
description: Lawyer Kamalpreet Chohan ran her finger down a list of 57 names of people scheduled to appear during a morning of hearings at the immigration court in California's capital and pointed out one glaring ...
fullText:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Lawyer Kamalpreet Chohan ran her finger down a list of 57 names of people scheduled to appear during a morning of hearings at the immigration court in California's capital and pointed out one glaring absence.

"None of these folks are represented," she said.

Chohan is the coordinator of a program that sends volunteer lawyers to immigration courts to assist people without representation and help them navigate the complicated legal system where the stakes are a future in America or deportation.

Appearing without a lawyer opens up even greater risk under the second Trump administration, with the courts playing a key role in its mass deportation agenda. Courts are increasingly denying asylum, deportation officers have arrested immigrants in court hallways, the administration has packed courtrooms to cut backlogs and reduced lead time on hearings, prompting people to miss them.

Data shows that legal representation can be vital to winning in court but many immigrants, unable to pay for a private lawyer or find a pro bono one, navigate the system without an attorney at their side.

"Folks go into immigration court not knowing what's happening. They come out not knowing what's happening. And when there's an attorney present," Chohan said, "it's just so helpful."

Unlike criminal court, there is no guaranteed lawyer in immigration courts.

Immigrants have to hire one at a cost of thousands of dollars or hope to get represented by one of the nonprofit organizations assisting low-income immigrants. But waitlists with those organizations are long, and many parts of the country just do not have that many immigration attorneys.

Of the roughly 3.2 million pending deportation cases currently in U.S. immigration courts, people in 52% of those cases do not have a lawyer, according to an analysis of immigration court data by the Vera Institute of Justice, a think tank.

A Congressional Research Service study from 2024 found that only 19% of people who did not have a lawyer won asylum or another avenue to stay in the United States. Among those who did have a lawyer, 47% were successful.

"Having an attorney is just super critical to be able to navigate the system successfully," said Adriel Orozco of the advocacy group American Immigration Council.

Chohan said she frequently runs into people who have been scammed by lawyers or people posing as lawyers who take their money but do nothing for their case.

"I will give him a list of attorneys who are free and we have vetted," she told one man who said he was scammed. "They have long waitlists but he should still ask."

Speaking later to The Associated Press, the man described how he left Guatemala after being threatened by gangs and came to the U.S. in 2024 seeking asylum. Ever since, he said he has done everything that has been asked of him while he tries to make ends meet, occasionally painting houses. He spent $4,500 on a lawyer who in the end did nothing to help him, he said.

"He turned out to be a scammer," said the man, who did not want to be identified for fear of endangering his case. He is worried about what comes next in court after being warned by the judge that he could be deported. "I don't know what I'm going to do," he said.

Outside the Sacramento building where the court is housed is a long line of immigrants waiting for appointments with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which is in the same building. Volunteers with a local anti-ICE resistance group stand ready to help.

Upstairs, two immigration judges are on the bench. One hears the in-depth individual cases of immigrants who are pursuing their claim of asylum.

The other judge has the master calendar docket, where dozens of immigrants will appear in brief hearings geared at making sure their case is ready to go to the next step.

Signs taped to the wall remind people not to videotape or record inside the court complex. A security guard makes sure no one loiters in the hallways. Most people clutch stacks of papers documenting their cases.

After immigrants file into the courtroom for their hearings, Judge Susan Phan introduces Chohan and describes the services her organization offers.

"You are not required to meet with her but it is a rare opportunity that we have someone volunteering their time," Phan said before launching into the day's work.

Chohan, who works with the California Immigration Project, starts each hearing in the courtroom. She has a clipboard to take notes, extra copies of forms and a crate of books for restless children attending court with their parents. She spends the bulk of her time in the waiting room, talking to immigrants after their hearings and scanning their documents to flesh out what else they need.

Speaking to one young man from Mexico, she asks to see his asylum application, noting that the judge had pointed out that it was not that detailed.

"Sometimes judges can deny a claim if there isn't enough detail," she said through one of the organization's volunteer translators.

The organization frequently has clinics to help immigrants fill out their asylum application. Chohan said she will alert him to the next one.

Another woman holding a stack of documents is there with her son and wanted to make sure her children could come with her if she is deported. Chohan also briefed her on what to expect at her upcoming asylum hearing and said the organization will send her an asylum filing guide.

Chohan highlighted places on forms where people need to give answers or answer in more detail. It's OK to write "none" but she advises them to not leave boxes blank.

Everything submitted in Spanish must be accompanied by a translation into English that must be done by a person, not an automatic online translator. Copies of every single page of a passport must be submitted. Documents must be sent in two weeks before the applicant's hearing so the judge can review them.

Over and over, Chohan reminds immigrants to download their receipt showing they paid the $102 asylum application fee so they can submit it to the court.

Chohan said a lot of these procedures and forms are discussed in court but it is happening so fast and immigrants are listening through a translator that they do not always understand what is happening.

"A lot of times when they go into court, they're just happy that they're out of court and they're not being arrested," she said.

Chohan has witnessed the upheaval in the immigration courts during Republican President Donald Trump's second term.

She was in the court hallways last summer when ICE officers waited to arrest immigrants after their hearings. Earlier this summer she watched as the administration started holding "mega masters," hearings with dozens of respondents at a time that are meant to clear a backlog but have created chaos.

Chohan said there are not enough pro bono lawyers in the Sacramento area to help everyone who needs one so the "Attorney of the Day" program is often the next best thing. She believes everyone should have access to a lawyer.

Until that day, she said, the program "helps bridge that gap."

title: California may fine content creators who don't disclose they were paid to post about politics
description: Weeks before voting ended in California's primary for governor, Los Angeles-based influencer Shaka Smith took to Instagram to tell his more than 700,000 followers whom he was voting for and why.  “Hea...
fullText:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Weeks before voting ended in California's primary for governor, Los Angeles-based influencer Shaka Smith took to Instagram to tell his more than 700,000 followers whom he was voting for and why.

"Healthcare shouldn't bankrupt you, housing should not feel impossible, polluters shouldn't pass their bill to us and artists should not be replaced by AI," Smith said. "That's why I'm supporting Tom Steyer for governor."

But Smith started the video with a disclaimer: "This is an ad, and honestly, I wish more political content said that first." His caption specified that he was paid by Steyer's campaign.

California is one of two states, along with Texas, that have passed policies requiring content creators to say if they've been paid by a political campaign to post, and the Golden State is considering cracking down by fining people who don't.

Campaigns have long worked with celebrities and major influencers to win over voters, but now they are teaming up with smaller creators — sometimes with fewer than 100,000 followers — to reach more tailored audiences. That has sparked debates about whether disclosure rules for political advertisements should apply to content creators, who are expected to play prominent roles in the upcoming midterms and the 2028 presidential election.

"If you're running for president and you are not currently trying to court some of these people or lining up your own people to act as surrogates for you, you're already behind," said Mike Nellis, a Democratic strategist who worked for Kamala Harris' presidential campaign.

Questions about transparency have been fueled by high-profile instances of influencers making content intended to change minds or votes without disclosing they were paid for it.

In 2022, the campaign of then-Senate candidate John Fetterman paid Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi of "Jersey Shore" to record a video teasing his GOP rival for leaving New Jersey before announcing his run in Pennsylvania. In 2023, content creators were paid by an influencer marketing agency with conservative ties to defend Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, after he was impeached for alleged bribery and other accusations of misconduct, according to the Texas Tribune. The payments weren't clearly disclosed in either case.

Steyer, a Democratic billionaire who spent more than $215 million of his own money in his unsuccessful bid for governor, took fire from rivals for paying content creators. He wasn't the only hopeful in the race paying influencers, but he faced much of the blowback since he'd already been accused of trying to buy the election. Many of the creators who worked with Steyer's campaign disclosed that they were paid, but the state's campaign finance watchdog is investigating several other instances in which creators allegedly didn't.

California Sen. Adam Schiff introduced federal legislation last month, but it hasn't received a vote yet. Some outside groups are urging the Federal Election Commission to pass its own rule.

California's law requiring disclosure, passed in 2023, is difficult to enforce. The state's campaign watchdog can seek a court order compelling an influencer to disclose that they were paid, but that can take months.

That prompted Democratic Assemblymember Marc Berman to write a new bill to penalize content creators and political committees if the creator fails to state they were compensated. The bill would give the state's Fair Political Practices Commission the power to fine influencers and committees if they are found to have violated the law, allowing the commission to bypass the court process. They could face fines of up to $5,000 per violation, according to the commission.

"Voters should have a right to know whether or not campaigns are paying for the messaging that they're seeing," Berman said.

Texas' campaign watchdog passed a rule in 2024 requiring content creators to include disclaimers when they are paid for political advertisements, and the New York Legislature is considering a similar requirement. Other disclosure bills failed in recent years in Utah and Georgia.

Smith, the L.A. influencer, hadn't committed to a candidate for governor when a trusted friend told him to look into Steyer. That friend had been paid to post about Steyer.

Smith liked Steyer's promise to increase taxes on billionaires and his refusal to accept donations from corporate political action committees.

He ended up doing two paid ads, both of which included compensation disclaimers that the Steyer campaign told him were a requirement.

Smith wouldn't say exactly how much the campaign paid him, but he said it was in the thousands of dollars. He thinks the posts had an impact on his followers, with only a few detractors pushing back.

"They kind of trust my voice," he said of his audience. "They knew that if I'm saying it, it's at least something they should look into."

Dustin Torreverde, a content creator in Southern California who hasn't been paid by a political campaign for social media posts, said it's important for influencers to be transparent with their audiences. But the bill could pose an unfair burden on creators who are just trying to make a living, he said.

"A lot of us are very small creators," he said. "So if we were to get penalized and we have to get lawyers, stuff like that, it's going to be very difficult for us."

Adina Flores, a libertarian content creator in Northern California who votes for both parties, said influencers should have to disclose if they are paid and she generally supports penalties. She worries that some people may take money to post political content without doing a "deep dive into the candidate to make sure that's somebody they should support."

Saurav Ghosh, a lawyer with the Campaign Legal Center, a nonprofit focused on protecting U.S. democracy, hopes disclosure requirements passed by states will lead to federal rules.

"Transparency is one of the most important pillars of our election system," he said.
